blocks.content: Every container moves through a small, well-defined set of states, created, running, possibly paused, stopped, and eventually removed, and a specific Docker command drives each transition.

A container is created (allocated, but not yet running), then running (its process is actually executing), then eventually stopped (the process exited or was killed, but the container still exists on disk), and finally removed (deleted entirely, writable layer and all).

blocks.alt: The four states most containers pass through

blocks.content: 2. Pausing Is a Special, Temporary State
blocks.text: 2. Pausing Is a Special, Temporary State

blocks.content: docker pause freezes every process in a container in place (using a cgroup freezer) without stopping them, and docker unpause resumes exactly where they left off. It is a less common tool, mostly useful for briefly freezing a container's CPU usage without losing its in-memory state.

blocks.alt: Paused freezes execution, it does not stop the container

blocks.content: 3. Stopping and Starting Again, Without Removing
blocks.text: 3. Stopping and Starting Again, Without Removing

blocks.content: A stopped container is not gone, docker start can bring the exact same container back to running, with its writable layer intact. This loop, stop and start, without ever removing, is one of the most common things you will do while developing locally.

blocks.alt: Stop and start again, same container, same writable layer

blocks.content: Each lifecycle transition has a specific, named command behind it, there is no ambiguity about which command does what once you know the state model.

blocks.alt: Each command maps to exactly one transition

blocks.content:
docker create nginx      # allocate, do not start yet
docker start <id>        # created -> running
docker stop <id>         # running -> stopped
docker rm <id>           # stopped -> gone

blocks.content: 5. The Full Path, End to End
blocks.text: 5. The Full Path, End to End

blocks.content: Put together, this is the complete life story of a container, from the moment it is allocated to the moment it no longer exists at all. Every command covered later in this module is really just a more convenient way of driving one of these same transitions.

blocks.alt: The complete path from creation to removal

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container moves through created, running, (optionally paused), stopped, and removed, each transition driven by a specific command.
A stopped container still exists, with its writable layer intact, until you explicitly remove it.
